e.t: Anchōch, also rendered Angghokh, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies one individual in the Greek Old Testament and does not carry a broader definition supplied by this record. The name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 6:45. Its precise significance belongs to the person and family setting in that passage, but the verse text is not available here for further explanation.

This word is a proper name, given as “Adōnai; Athone.” It identifies a named designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 1:11. The available lexical wording supplies the name itself but does not provide a broader ordinary-language definition. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage, while the word’s basic function is to serve as a proper name.

Ἀθηνόβιος is a proper name, rendered as Athēnobios or Athinovios. It identifies a particular person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the name occurs twice, both times in 1 Maccabees 15, at 15:28 and 15:32. The name itself gives the person’s identity; understanding what he does or why he appears requires the surrounding verse and passage.

This proper name refers to Ethiopia, a place named in the Greek Old Testament. The word identifies a geographic region rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. It appears 15 times in the Greek Old Testament, across books including Genesis, Esther, Job, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and Zephaniah. Its precise geographic reference in any particular passage depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains the name Ethiopia.

This adjective means “unsettled,” describing something lacking stability, calm, or settled condition. It presents the idea of being disturbed or not firmly established, rather than secure and at rest. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 54:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a condition of instability or disturbance.

This word means “another” or “else,” referring to a different person, thing, or choice. It can describe someone or something distinct from what has already been mentioned, and it may also stand in as a pronoun for an alternative person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 79 times, showing a broad and ordinary use for expressing distinction or an additional possibility. Its precise force in a verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This proper noun refers to an Ammanite, identifying a member of the Ammanite people. It is a group name rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: once in Deuteronomy and twice in Nehemiah. Its exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and passage context.

This Greek LXX verb means “straighten up,” describing the action of lifting oneself from a bent or lowered posture. It presents a physical movement rather than a name or description of a person. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus represented here, once in Job and once in Susanna. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the act of straightening upward.

This Greek LXX verb means to “act against” or “seek to counteract” someone or something. It describes active opposition rather than simple disagreement: the person using it is working against an action, plan, or opposing force. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 14:29. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains deliberate resistance or an attempt to prevent another purpose from succeeding.

This Greek LXX verb means “go off,” describing someone or something moving away or departing. Its basic sense is an action of leaving rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs six times in the LXX corpus, in Job, Proverbs, Hosea, and Wisdom. The surrounding sentence determines whether the departure is physical or refers more generally to being absent or removed.

This verb means “deal cruelly with”: it describes treating someone harshly, without kindness or consideration. As a verb, it expresses an action done to another rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Job 39:16. The word’s basic sense is therefore a forceful description of cruel treatment; the surrounding verse determines exactly who acts and who receives that treatment.

This adverb means “compactly” or “closely,” describing an action done in a tightly joined or concentrated way. It modifies another word by showing how something is arranged or carried out, rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:4. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what it describes there, but its basic sense is firm: something is brought together, held, or performed closely and without looseness.

This Greek LXX verb means to dine or have a meal. It describes the act of eating a meal rather than naming the food itself. Its stated sense includes “dine” and “each meal,” so it can refer generally to meal-eating. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Kings 13:7. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is to dine or eat a meal.

“Asa” is a personal name used for people identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general word describing an object, action, or quality, but as a proper name. The name occurs 55 times across 47 Old Testament verses, especially in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles. Its exact reference—whether to a particular person named Asa—depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical meaning supplied for the name is simply “Asa.”

This word is a proper name, presented in English as “Asouēros” or “Asoiros.” It identifies a specific named figure or subject rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 4:6. The name itself supplies identification, while the surrounding verse and passage determine who is being named and what role that person has in the account.

This LXX Greek adjective means “secure,” describing someone or something as safe, dependable, or firmly protected. It presents security as a condition of stability rather than danger or uncertainty. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, including Proverbs and Wisdom. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains being secure and able to stand safely. It is distinct here as an LXX word, not a Greek New Testament entity.

Baithmachereb, also given as Vethmakherev, is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Joshua 19:5, so its precise referent must be understood from that passage rather than from a broad range of uses. No wider lexical sense is given beyond these name forms.

This adjective describes someone as “heavy” or “slow of heart,” expressing an inward dullness or heaviness rather than physical weight. It is a descriptive word for a person whose heart is not quick or responsive. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 4:3. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to a heart weighed down or slow to respond. Its approved meaning is “heavy; slow of heart.”

Bēsana, also rendered Visana, is a proper name preserved as Besana in English Bible tradition. It does not function like a common noun describing an action, quality, or object; it identifies a particular named person or location, though the available information does not establish which in Joshua 18:22. This LXX word occurs once, in Joshua 18:22, so its meaning is chiefly its identifying name rather than a broader concept.

This verb means to drink milk. It describes the act of consuming milk as a drink, rather than naming the milk itself or a person who drinks it. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 13:21. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains straightforward: taking milk as nourishment or refreshment by drinking it.

This word means “scripture,” referring to sacred writing or a written text that carries scriptural authority. It is a noun used for Scripture as something recorded in writing, rather than merely spoken teaching. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it occurs 38 times, including passages about Israel’s written ordinances and sacred records. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains written Scripture.

This word means “sixteen,” the number that comes after fifteen and before seventeen. It functions as a number word, identifying a quantity rather than a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:41. Its basic meaning is precise and does not require a broader symbolic sense here; the surrounding verse determines what group or quantity of sixteen is being identified.

This Greek LXX verb means “burn through; heat to excess.” It describes intense burning or heating beyond what is ordinary, emphasizing the force or extreme degree of the heat. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 4 Maccabees 11:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is burning intensely or becoming excessively hot.

gl: reckon up one by one; enumerate
d: reckon up one by one; enumerate

e.t: This verb means to reckon up items one by one—to count or enumerate them individually. It describes a deliberate process of going through a group or list and numbering its parts rather than treating everything as one undivided whole. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:6. The exact force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on careful, item-by-item counting.

gl: have a way out; break away
d: have a way out; break away

e.t: This verb means to have a way out or to break away. It describes the act of finding or making an exit rather than remaining confined or held in place. As a verb, it expresses movement toward escape or release. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Daniel 3:48. The word’s basic sense is therefore focused and concrete: something or someone gets out, breaks free, or finds a means of leaving. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly how that action functions there.

This word means “twelve,” the number that comes after eleven and before thirteen. It functions as an indeclinable number, used to state a count or identify a group, set, or quantity of twelve. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 90 times, so its basic meaning remains consistent across many passages. The word itself gives a number; the surrounding verse determines what people, objects, or groups are being counted.

This verb means “beget” or “bring forth”: it describes producing or bringing someone into existence. As a verb, it points to the act of generation rather than naming the person produced. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 109:3. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here, but its central meaning remains the act of begetting or bringing forth.

This verb means to redeem someone by paying a ransom. It describes release obtained through a payment made on behalf of the person being freed, emphasizing both the act of redemption and its cost. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Numbers 3:49, so its precise use there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word presents redemption as a deliberate transaction that secures release rather than merely expressing a general wish to help or rescue.

This Greek verb means “model.” It describes forming or shaping something according to a model or pattern. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Exodus, where it belongs to descriptions of crafted items and their design. Its central idea is that something is made with a specified form rather than left without shape. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the word consistently points to modeling or giving form.

Elkai, also rendered “Elke,” is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Nehemiah 12:15. Because it is a proper name, its significance comes from the person it identifies in that passage, not from a broader dictionary idea or repeated scriptural usage.

This noun means “outward appearance; impression”—the way something presents itself or the effect it makes on someone. It points to what is perceived from the outside, rather than necessarily describing a thing’s inner reality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:8. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is the visible or perceived impression something gives.

Enath is a proper name, referring to a specific place or location rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 19:34. The available lexical meaning is simply “Enath,” so its significance comes from the place it identifies in that passage and its surrounding list of boundaries. This name should remain distinct as a Greek LXX word and should not be treated as a general word with several meanings.

This word means “six,” identifying a quantity of six items, people, days, or other counted things. It functions as a number rather than naming an object or action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 1,011 times, showing regular use wherever Scripture gives a count or measurement. Its exact reference—whether to people, objects, time, or another quantity—depends on the surrounding verse, but the numerical meaning remains six.

“Houseless” describes someone or something without a home or dwelling. It is an adjective, so it identifies a person or thing by the absence of a place to live. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Job 6:18. The word’s basic meaning is therefore focused and specific: being without a house or settled dwelling. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains the lack of a home.

This verb means “laugh at” or “exult over”—to respond to another person with mocking amusement or triumphant delight. It describes an attitude expressed toward someone else, rather than ordinary laughter that is simply joyful. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 5:27. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic sense concerns ridiculing someone or taking pleasure in that person’s misfortune.

The word means “set on,” describing an action in which something is placed upon or directed onto something else. It functions as a verb, so it expresses what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or quality. This LXX word occurs three times, each in a different Old Testament verse: Deuteronomy 24:15, Joshua 8:29, and Jeremiah 15:9. Its basic sense remains the same across these occurrences, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being set on and how the action functions there.

This Greek LXX noun means “preparation”: the act or condition of making something ready. It can describe readiness for an action, an arranged setting, or what has been made prepared. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented in this LXX corpus, including uses in Ezra, Psalms, Nahum, Zechariah, and Wisdom. Its central idea remains practical readiness rather than a specific object or event; the surrounding verse determines what is being prepared. “Preparation” is also the attested English rendering in several occurrences.

This word means “spear,” a long weapon with a pointed head used for thrusting or throwing. It is a noun naming a physical weapon, and its plural form can refer to more than one spear. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Isaiah and once in Jeremiah. The word itself identifies the weapon, while the surrounding verse determines how that weapon functions in the passage. Its basic meaning remains concrete and straightforward: a spear used as an instrument of warfare or combat.

This word means “I was,” expressing a speaker’s or writer’s existence or condition in the past. It functions as a first-person expression, referring to the person speaking or being described rather than to someone else. In the Greek LXX, it occurs 42 times across 38 verses, showing that it is a recurring way to state what someone previously was or how someone previously existed. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Tharsila is a proper name, referring to a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its lexical meaning is simply “Tharsila,” so it should be understood as a personal designation, not translated into a broader concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 15:14. The available information identifies the name but does not provide additional details about the person or the name’s significance in that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “hunt; catch.” It describes actively pursuing something with the aim of capturing it, rather than merely seeing or searching for it. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament wording represented here, at Psalms 139:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the sentence uses the verb. The related English rendering is “hunt,” which fits the central idea of pursuit leading to capture.

Iadae, also given as Iathae, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than naming an action, quality, place, or object. This name occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in 1 Chronicles 2—at verses 28 and 32. The name itself is the word’s meaning here; no further ordinary-language definition or name-meaning is provided. Its precise reference in each genealogy depends on the surrounding verse text.

Ianoka is a proper name, rendered as “Ianōka; Ianoka.” It identifies a particular named person or place in the Greek Old Testament text rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Joshua 16:6. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be described further here, but its lexical function is clear: it serves as a personal or place-name designation.

This word is a proper name referring to a person called Jeremiah. It is a personal designation rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, it occurs 113 times, most often in the book bearing Jeremiah’s name. The same name also appears in historical and other biblical passages, identifying Jeremiah wherever he is mentioned. Its meaning here is therefore the person’s name, and the surrounding verse determines what is being said about him in each occurrence.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Iesou” or “Iesu.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Numbers 26:28. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the name’s specific referent in that passage cannot be clarified further here. Its basic function is simply to name an individual.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Iōadae” or “Ioathae.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 12:28. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide an additional descriptive meaning or explanation of the person. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its place in the account.

This Greek LXX noun means “season” or “opportunity.” It refers to a fitting period or a favorable occasion for something to happen or be done. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly, appearing 411 times across 360 verses, so its precise sense depends on the sentence around it. It can describe recurring seasons, such as those mentioned in Genesis and Leviticus, or an opportunity presented in a situation. This is an LXX Greek word and should remain distinct from Greek New Testament word entries.

This verb means “denounce”: to openly accuse or condemn someone. It describes a forceful act of speaking against a person, rather than merely mentioning a fault or expressing private disagreement. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs three times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 1 and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding words and situation, but its central sense remains a public or serious declaration against someone.

This verb means to “look down”—to direct one’s gaze downward. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Exodus 3:6. The word describes the physical action of lowering or directing the eyes, while the surrounding verse determines why the person looks down and what that action signifies there. Its basic meaning is therefore visual and directional: the eyes are turned downward rather than toward something level or above.

Kelez is a proper name, used as a personal designation rather than as a general descriptive word. In the Greek LXX, it appears once, and its recorded rendering is “Kelez.” The occurrence is found at Joshua 17:2, but no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, so the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be explained further. Its meaning is therefore the name itself: Kelez.

This verb means “practise divination”—to seek knowledge or guidance through divination rather than through ordinary understanding. It describes an activity, not merely a prediction or a passing thought. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: once in Deuteronomy and once each in 2 Kings and 2 Chronicles. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the practice of divination.

This noun means “anything round,” referring to something shaped in a circle or having a rounded form. It describes physical form rather than an action or quality of character. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times across five verses, including passages in 2 Chronicles, Job, Psalms, and Ezekiel. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a round or circular object or feature.

This word means “cake,” referring to a prepared food made in a rounded or flattened form. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament for a baked food presented or eaten in various passages. The word occurs nine times in the LXX, all within Old Testament verses, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise use in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This proper noun refers to the Libyes, also rendered Livies. It is the name of a people mentioned in the Greek Old Testament, rather than a general description or action. The word occurs eight times in the LXX, appearing in passages from 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and Nahum. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the designation of this named people.

Lysias is a proper name identifying a particular man, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it refers to the person named Lysias and appears 24 times, chiefly in 1 and 2 Maccabees. The name is rendered consistently as “Lysias,” with “Lisias” also given as a spelling variant. Its precise role in any passage depends on the surrounding context.

Manēs, also rendered Manis, is a proper name referring to a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament-related corpus represented here, it appears once, at 4 Maccabees 10:13. The name itself identifies the individual, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand that person’s role or significance there. Thus, its basic meaning is a personal name, not a description or title.

This Greek LXX noun means “breast,” referring to the part of the body associated with nourishment and the female form. It is used in the Greek translation of the Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, including descriptions of women, children, and bodily imagery. The word occurs 35 times in the LXX corpus, with especially frequent use in Song of Songs. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the breast or breasts of a person or animal.

This verb means “nod”: to make a movement of the head that communicates or signals something. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, both in Proverbs. The exact force of a particular occurrence depends on the surrounding verse, but the word’s central idea remains the act of nodding.

This word means “insincerely” or “disingenuously,” describing speech or action that is not genuine or straightforward. As an adverb, it explains how someone speaks or acts, pointing to a lack of honest intent rather than merely an accidental mistake. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is conduct that appears sincere while actually being deceptive or false.

This adjective describes something destructive or deadly—something marked by ruin, severe harm, or the power to cause death. It functions as a describing word, adding this quality to a person, thing, action, or condition in its sentence. In the LXX corpus, it occurs four times across four verses, so its basic sense is consistent but its precise force depends on what it describes in each passage. The word appears in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings represented in this Greek corpus.

Orna is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 22 times across 19 verses, chiefly in 1 Chronicles and 2 Samuel. Because it functions as a personal name, its meaning is identifying: it distinguishes Orna from other people in the surrounding account. The name is rendered consistently as “Orna,” and no broader lexical sense is provided for it.

This verb means being “governed by passion”: strong feelings or desires control a person’s actions. It describes a state in which passion exercises authority over someone, rather than merely being present as an emotion. In the Greek LXX corpus, this verb occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 7:20. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central meaning is being ruled or directed by passion.

This adverb means “altogether” or “absolutely,” expressing a complete or unqualified extent. It strengthens the statement it accompanies, indicating that something is wholly so rather than partly or in a limited way. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, all in nine different verses, with six occurrences in Ezekiel and single occurrences in 1 Kings, Jeremiah, and Zephaniah. Its exact force in any sentence is determined by the words and situation around it.

This verb describes someone as deranged or as having gone mad. It expresses a condition of mental disturbance rather than an ordinary change of mood or opinion. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Hosea 9:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a strong description of someone whose judgment or behavior has become disordered.

This Greek LXX noun means “coat,” referring to a garment worn on the body. It names a physical item of clothing rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, across ten verses, from Exodus through Ezekiel. Its exact significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “turn sideways,” describing a change from a direct position or direction to one angled to the side. It refers to the act of shifting position rather than remaining straightforward or face-to-face. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 29:21. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself expresses sideways movement or orientation.

This verb means “assure”: to give someone confidence or certainty about something. It describes an act of assuring rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Ecclesiastes 8:11. The available lexical meaning identifies its central sense clearly, while the precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its sentence context.

This Greek LXX verb means “toil”: to work with effort, exertion, or weariness. It describes labor rather than simply naming an activity, and its precise force in a sentence depends on what kind of work the surrounding passage describes. The word occurs 38 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, showing that it is used across several settings rather than being limited to one subject. Its earliest listed occurrence is Genesis 34:25, and its latest is 4 Maccabees 18:2.

This Greek LXX verb means “red” or “enflamed,” describing something that has become visibly flushed, fiery, or reddened. It expresses a change into that condition rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, in Lamentations 4:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic idea remains becoming red or enflamed.

Raphaim, also rendered Rhafem, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 23:13. The name identifies a particular person, group, or place in that passage, but the name itself does not explain the surrounding event or provide a broader definition. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from the verse and its context. The spelling Raphaim or Rhafem preserves the name as a distinct designation.

Raphia is a proper place name. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 1:1. Because it names a location rather than describing an action, quality, or object, its basic meaning is simply the place called Raphia. The name itself does not provide further information about the location or its significance; those details must come from the surrounding passage and wider scriptural context.

This word is the name “Reuben.” As a noun, it identifies rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears 87 times in the LXX corpus, from Genesis through Ezekiel, showing repeated use across Israel’s historical and genealogical material. Its precise significance in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical meaning remains the personal name Reuben.

“Roman” refers to a person belonging to Rome or associated with the Roman people. It is a noun used as a group designation, identifying Romans rather than describing an action or quality. In this Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings corpus, the word occurs 13 times, especially in 1 and 2 Maccabees, and once in Daniel. Its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it appears: a Roman person or people. The surrounding passage determines what is being said about them in any particular verse.

Samarani is a proper name, referring to a person named Samarani. It is not presented here as a general descriptive word or action, but as an identifying name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Numbers 26:20. The name itself supplies the meaning available here; understanding the person’s specific identity or role requires the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included in this word-level entry.

This adjective means “made of flesh; fleshy.” It describes something characterized by or consisting of flesh, rather than naming an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times across five verses, including passages in 2 Chronicles, Esther, Proverbs, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains connected with flesh or a fleshy quality.

Sarra is a personal name used to identify a particular person. As a proper noun in the Greek LXX, it names rather than describes an action, quality, or object. The word occurs 37 times in the LXX corpus, almost entirely in Genesis, with one occurrence in Isaiah. Its ordinary meaning is therefore the name “Sarra,” while the surrounding verse determines what is being said about her in each passage.

This noun refers to a “cucumber bed,” a cultivated place where cucumbers grow. It describes a planted garden plot rather than the vegetable itself. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice, once in Isaiah and once in the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its basic meaning is specific and concrete: a field or patch prepared for growing cucumbers. The surrounding verse determines why that image is used in each passage.

This word is a proper name for “Sousa,” also known as “Susa.” It identifies the same named place throughout the Greek Old Testament passages where it appears, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 16 verses, with most occurrences in Esther. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and its role there.

This Greek LXX verb means “drop” or “let fall.” It describes something falling from a person or object, or being caused to fall. The word appears 16 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, across 14 verses, and can refer to literal drops as well as something being released or lowered. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is described as falling and the surrounding sentence.

This noun refers to “hard meat”—meat that is tough or difficult to chew. It names a physical kind of food rather than an action, person, or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears only once, in Job 20:18. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise force in that passage cannot be described further; its ordinary lexical meaning remains “hard meat.”

This Greek LXX verb means “press”: it describes the act of pushing or bearing against something with force. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 27:12. That reference identifies its only occurrence, but without the verse text its particular force there cannot be described more specifically. Its central meaning remains the act of pressing.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Sōcha” or “Sokha.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:48.
